doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Eurosuite and Friedrich Gulda's orchestra
summary: Eurosuite was first written for Gulda's European band and re-recorded for a reduced big band.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Eurosuite. That was the second album. [The Total J. J. Johnson]

That was the second album, yeah. Eurosuite came about under interesting circumstances. Classical pianist Friedrich Gulda was also a very good jazz pianist and had a keen interest in jazz, even though his forte was as a classical musician and as a

classical pianist. But he put together a jazz band to tour in Europe. I don’t know what year that was. [In the discography of The Musical World of J. J. Johnson by Joshua Berrett and Louis Bourgois III there is a listing for two days of recording on September 13-14, 1965 in Vienna, Austria by Friedrich Gulda and His Euro-Orchestra; both J. J. Johnson and Freddie Hubbard are listed in the personnel.] Dave, what [was the] approximate . . .
I just remember you and Freddie [Hubbard] were two of the main soloists on it.
And Ron Carter, yes. Sorry about that.
Oh, wait. It wasn’t Freddie. It was Art Farmer.

Beautiful, beautiful Art Farmer. The three soloists from the United States were myself, Art Farmer, and Ron Carter. The work featured the three of us, for the most part. Friedrich Gulda wrote a wonderful piece. I wrote my piece called Eurosuite, which was a suite in four or five movements, for that occasion. I re-recorded it under the circumstances that you just spoke about.
On the second album. [Two excerpts from Eurosuite were released as Euro #1 and Euro #2 on the album The Total J. J. Johnson. Art Farmer is on this recording.]
On the second album, right. I re-voiced it even, because interestingly enough, that wasn’t your standard big band.

It wasn’t. It was big band, but not your standard big band. Whereas the standard big band has five saxes, four trumpets, four trombones, [and] a rhythm section, the band that we are talking about now had three saxes, two trumpets, two trombones, and a rhythm section. It was quite a challenge to pare down and yet try to project this big band image. It was a challenge that I enjoyed, working on that. The arrangements worked out very well.
